overview: This Mysore record covers 1815 to 1878, after the Wodeyar dynasty’s restoration in 1799. Its coarse outline includes Mysuru and Bengaluru but cannot show their changing jurisdictions. Royal government gave way to British commissioners in 1831; the return of administration to the dynasty in 1881 lies beyond the map’s endpoint. The earlier Mysore card covers Tipu Sultan and the 1799 transition.

periods.title: Royal administration
periods.summary: Krishnaraja Wodeyar III governed within the restored, British-dependent kingdom.

periods.title: British commissioners
periods.summary: British officials took over administration; the royal house remained.

periods.title: A young successor
periods.summary: Chamarajendra succeeded by adoption in 1868, while commissioners continued to govern.

items.text: British authorities justified taking over Mysore’s administration in 1831 by citing rebellion and alleged misgovernment. This was a transfer of effective power, not the disappearance of the royal family. Later histories dispute the colonial justification, so the change should not be described simply as a benevolent rescue.

The restoration of administration in 1881 came after this card’s dates. Maharaja Chamarajendra received ruling powers on 25 March, with Rangacharlu as diwan. A Representative Assembly followed inOctober. These were important institutional changes, but an elite consultative assembly was not universal voting rights.

Rice’s 1877 gazetteer describes low earthen houses with inward-facing courtyards and verandahs. Wealthier homes could have paved, drained courts and carved wooden pillars; poorer roofs were often thatched. The courtyard brought daylight into homes with few outward-facing openings.

Ragi was a major staple. The gazetteer’s report for 1874 to 1875 notes that its price rose despite a good harvest, while rice and some pulses became cheaper. A family’s food budget could depend on which grain it relied upon.

The local Anche post relied on runners: in 1875 to 1876 its routes totaled 2,312 miles, linking 152 receiving offices. Private letters, newspapers and official dispatches traveled through a relay of runners.
The 1868 village-school scheme proposed night classes for people unable to attend during working hours. Pupils would pay for lighting. Learning after work meant finding both time and a lamp.

Maharaja’s College grew from a free school founded in 1833. The government took over the school in 1868, and college affiliation followed in 1879, after this map interval. Separating those dates avoids putting later university buildings and courses into an earlier classroom.

Bengaluru’s Literary and Scientific Institute began in 1868 on Museum Road. It later became the Bowring Institute. Its history is a reminder that adult learning also took place in associations; the institution’s familiar later building belongs to a different phase, beyond 1878.

Bowring Hospital began admitting patients in 1868. Rice describes a plan adapted from a Paris hospital, with space to separate disease categories and caste groups. Medical buildings could expand treatment while also reproducing social divisions; a hospital was not automatically an equal space.

Bengaluru’s military settlement and adjoining neighborhoods shared connected water systems. In the 1860s, investigators found that rainy-season overflow could wash sewage toward wells. A boundary between jurisdictions did not stop dirty water: drainage problems needed attention across the whole area.

Some slopes near horse-keepers’ and grass-cutters’ homes served as public latrines. Officials seeking healthier barracks proposed removing nearby homes. The history of sanitation therefore includes a hard question: who received protection, and who risked losing a place to live?

Water engineers tried different solutions. An 1865 proposal would have collected rain from barrack roofs in underground reservoirs, but officials chose another scheme. This was a proposed system, not a household service that everyone actually received.

The 1870s famine was also a water emergency. Families faced drying wells and tanks while some people resorted to ditches and puddles. Contemporary reporting contrasted water carted for troops and horses with inadequate help for residents. Hunger, disease and unequal access reinforced one another.

sections.title: Games and writing you can inspect

items.text: Manuscripts associated with Krishnaraja Wadiyar III preserve a tiger game with two tiger pieces facing 25 people. The sides have different jobs: tigers jump to capture, while the people try to block them. Being outnumbered does not necessarily make the tiger the underdog!

The game’s board combines a square grid with triangles attached to its sides. Players follow marked lines, and the people are placed before they can move. Surviving diagrams preserve a form of practical reasoning: planning space, anticipating an opponent and turning a drawing into play.

A twenty-cash coin dated 1833 carries the Kannada name ಕೃಷ್ಣ, transcribed Kṛṣṇa, or Krishna. It names the ruler in the catalogue’s reading. The short sample is a modern Unicode rendering of an attested coin inscription, verified in the government museum’s 1889 catalogue.

That small 1833 coin mixes Kannada, Persian and English lettering, including XX CASH for its value. Money moved among readers of different languages. A coin could advertise a ruler, identify a mint and state a denomination in very little space.

Writing in 1908 about collecting in the 1890s, R. P. Jackson recalled villagers bringing him old coins and sometimes asking whether he was exchanging them officially for new money. Objects that now sit in collections once had owners, prices and uncertain futures outside museums.

Karnataka’s archives preserve Mysore government proceedings from 1843 and gazettes from 1866, alongside commissioners’ files and manuscripts in several languages. These records allow historians to investigate government beyond palace portraits: decisions, correspondence and administration also left evidence.

ending.text: The atlas ends in 1878 while British commissioners still governed. Administration returned to Chamarajendra in 1881, under continuing British paramountcy. Mysore’s institutions and communities continued beyond that transition; the map endpoint is not the kingdom’s extinction.
